query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Phase-selective recrystallization can overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness in eutectic high-entropy alloys while retaining or increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies
generation.conditions: Room temperature, quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests
generation.structural_mediator: Semi-coherent phase boundaries and the proportion of FCC/BCC phases
generation.mechanism: Dislocation strengthening without ductility trade-off, potent impediments from chemically disordered semi-coherent phase boundaries
generation.predicted_outcome: Uniform elongation of ∼33% and an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching ∼2.2 GPa
generation.baseline: As-cast alloy with a fracture strength of ~0.94 GPa and ductility of ~25%
generation.boundary: Limitations in ductility due to dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between phase-selective recrystallization, semi-coherent phase boundaries, and dislocation strengthening mechanisms is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phase-selectively recrystallized alloy does not exhibit a uniform elongation of ∼33% and an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching ∼2.2 GPa, the hypothesis is falsified

Question: How do semi-coherent phase boundaries and the proportion of FCC/BCC phases influence the strengthening mechanism and mechanical properties in a eutectic dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.4 (eutectic dual-phase HEA with BCC and FCC lamellar phases). Processing: Vacuum arc melting of pure elements (Al, Co, Ni, Cr, Fe) at 1773 K, repeated melting at least five times with electromagnetic stirring, and solidification in a water-cooled copper hearth; some samples were cold rolled for pre-straining.. Test conditions: In situ tensile tests inside a TEM at a strain rate of ~1.0 μm∙s−1 with 200 kV accelerating voltage; room-temperature tensile tests using an Instron 5569 machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1.. Own digest: Paper card. Question: How can the limited ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) be overcome to achieve ultra-ductility while maintaining high strength?. System: Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy consisting of FCC and B2 phases; industrial A357 casting aluminum alloy. Processing: Two cycles of 30% cold rolling followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 20 mins with water quenching; for A357: two cycles of 15% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins followed by two cycles of 30% cold rolling at 540 °C for 40 mins. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ tensile tests in FE-SEM; loading-unloading-reloading tests for back stress measurement.
